```{=html}
The project has two phases, and so does this report:
  Phase 1, the replication. Introduction and Methods are written, critiqued and preregistered
           BEFORE data collection; the Methods addendum, Results and Discussion after it.
  Phase 2, the extension. Proposed after Phase 1 (Rationale, Changes from Phase 1, Power and
           sample, Analysis plan), then run, with its own Results and Discussion.
The AI use statement and the Key statistics table sit at the top and are kept current
throughout. Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas for Phase 2.

Render this file at every stage. Before a phase has data, its results say so and skip
themselves; during Pilot A the Phase 1 results run on pilot data, which is the point of Pilot A.

Grey "Guidance" boxes are instructions. Delete each one once you have written that section.
```

```{r}
pilot_mode <- FALSE

# Stopping rule from the preregistration: recruitment stopped at 260 people who pass the
# exclusion rule. The last batch of Prolific places overshot, so more than 260 passed. I analyse

analysis_n <- if (pilot_mode) Inf else 260

analysis_n2 <- if (pilot_mode) Inf else 386
# In pilot mode the model has no control variables (see fit_outcome), so the caption says so.
model_note <- if (pilot_mode) "no control variables in the pilot model" else
```

```{r}
#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figure.
# Source: Osborne, Brown & Sillence (2026), JMIR Formative Research, 10:e85788.
#
# Sample: 749 people took part; 4 + 8 were excluded, so N = 737 were analysed.
# Groups: normal = 248, distress = 241, transformative = 248.
orig_n <- c(normal = 248, distress = 241, transformative = 248)

# Worry ratings (1-5) in the two conditions of the key test, calculated from the original
# authors' shared data on OSF (https://osf.io/gnb2e) after their exclusions. Used below to
# get Cohen's d directly from means and SDs.
orig_worry <- tribble(~condition, ~n,  ~mean,    ~sd,"normal",   248, 2.532258, 1.033335, "distress", 241, 2.991701, 1.064549)

# Ordinal logistic regression results for "distress vs normal" (the comparison group is
# normal). beta = log-odds coefficient (the effect size), se = its standard error,
# z = beta / se. Outcomes were rated on a 5-point scale.
original <- tribble(
  ~outcome,       ~beta,   ~se,    ~z,
  "worried",       0.910,  0.170,  5.350,
  "reassured",    -0.970,  0.167, NA,
  "confused",      0.818,  0.170, NA,
  "optimistic",   -0.708,  0.165, NA,
  "anxious",       0.817,  0.168, NA,
  "empowered",    -0.540,  0.162, NA,
  "knowledgeable", 0.564,  0.163, NA,
  "liked",        -0.864,  0.171, NA
)
# Our key analysis: worried, distress vs normal.
original_key <- original |> filter(outcome == "worried")
```

# AI use statement

I used ChatGPT and Claude (Sonnet 5.5) to help me with the experiment,
code, tests and the calculations for the power analysis. They explained
some statistical procedures to me and how to use RStudio, git, Quarto
and Firebase. They gave me feedback and corrections for my writing,
grammar, spelling, and tense, and gave me examples of sentences. They
also helped me to add my text to the report and delete the guidance
boxes. I checked what the AI told me by searching on the internet, the
course Experimentology online book, checking on my own what the code
chunks meant, and double-checking everything.

I used Claude to help me read and understand the authors’ analysis code
and make my model formula the same as theirs. I used their data to
calculate the descriptive statistics and check the main result. Claude
also helped me add a filter in the experiment code using the age and
menopause questions that were already there. With this filter,
participants who did not meet the criteria could not continue the study.

In Phase 2, I used Claude to add the new pages for the STAI-6, the word association task, the questions about expected symptoms, and the menopause mindset items. I also used it to write an automated test and to help with the Phase 2 analysis code.

Claude helped draft the prompt for the spelling check. Claude Sonnet 5.5 will be used once to suggest spelling corrections from a list of unique responses. The list will have no participant IDs or group labels. Andrea Morales Leal will check the suggestions before they are used. AFINN will be used to score the responses.

# Key statistics

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# Turn one survey page's answers into columns. jsPsych saves each page's answers as one JSON
# string, for example {"worried":2,"reassured":1,...}. This unpacks that string for one task.
parse_task <- function(trials, task_name) {
  one <- trials |> filter(task == task_name)
  if (nrow(one) == 0) return(tibble(participant_id = character()))
  one |>
    mutate(resp = map(response, ~ fromJSON(.x))) |>
    select(participant_id, resp) |>
    unnest_wider(resp)
}

# The 5 answer choices of the social media use question, in order (Never = 1 ... Several times
# per day = 5). Used to turn the answer into a number for the model.
social_levels <- c("Never", "Less than weekly", "Weekly", "Daily", "Several times per day")

# Column names of the Phase 2 scales (they match the names in experiment.js).
stai_items    <- c("stai_calm", "stai_tense", "stai_upset", "stai_relaxed", "stai_content", "stai_worried")
mindset_items <- c("mindset_opportunity", "mindset_decline", "mindset_important",
                   "mindset_enjoyable", "mindset_nothing_to_look_forward", "mindset_manageable")

# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that phase
# has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id, max_n = Inf) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  # Drop my own test sessions (see test_ids at the top).
  participants <- participants |> filter(!participant_id %in% test_ids)
  trials       <- trials       |> filter(!participant_id %in% test_ids)
  # People who declined the consent form. The export marks them as "completed" (the study
  # ends right after the refusal), but they saw no posts and gave no ratings, so they are not
  # counted as completers. consented is TRUE/FALSE on the consent trial, empty elsewhere.
  refused <- if ("consented" %in% names(trials)) {
    trials |>
      filter(task == "consent", tolower(as.character(consented)) == "false") |>
      pull(participant_id) |> unique()
  } else character(0)
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()

  # Keep only people who finished the study, and compute how many minutes they took
  # (end time minus start time; the times are saved as text like 2026-10-15T22:29:55Z).
  complete <- participants |>
    filter(completed, !participant_id %in% refused) |>
    mutate(minutes = as.numeric(difftime(lubridate::ymd_hms(ended_at),
                                         lubridate::ymd_hms(started_at), units = "mins")))
  # If nobody has finished yet (for example only my own test sessions exist), treat the phase
  # as "no data yet" so the rest of the report skips itself instead of failing.
  if (nrow(complete) == 0) return(NULL)

  # One row per completed participant: condition, demographics, and every rating.
  # jsPsych saves the 5-point answers as 0-4, so 1 is added to put them back on 1-5.
  tr <- trials |> filter(participant_id %in% complete$participant_id)
  rating_cols <- c("liked", "credible", "trust", "empowered", "knowledgeable",
                   "worried", "reassured", "confused", "in_control", "optimistic", "anxious")
  dat <- complete |>
    select(participant_id, condition, minutes, started_at) |>
    left_join(parse_task(tr, "demographics"), by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(parse_task(tr, "ratings_agree"), by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(parse_task(tr, "ratings_feel"), by = "participant_id") |>
    # Phase 2 pages (these tasks do not exist in Phase 1 data, so nothing is added there)
    left_join(parse_task(tr, "stai6"), by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(parse_task(tr, "symptom_expectation"), by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(parse_task(tr, "mindsets"), by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(
      across(any_of(c(rating_cols, stai_items, mindset_items)), ~ as.numeric(.x) + 1),
      age                 = as.numeric(age),
      education_years     = as.numeric(education_years),
      social_media_use    = match(social_media_use, social_levels),
      condition           = factor(condition, levels = c("normal", "distress"))
    )

  # STAI-6 score (Phase 2 only). The items are now 1-4. Reverse-score calm, relaxed and content
  # (5 minus the answer), add all six, multiply by 20 and divide by 6: range 20 to 80.
  if (all(stai_items %in% names(dat))) {
    dat <- dat |>
      mutate(stai_score = ((5 - stai_calm) + stai_tense + stai_upset +
                           (5 - stai_relaxed) + (5 - stai_content) + stai_worried) * 20 / 6)
  }

  # Menopause mindset score (Phase 2 only). The items are now 1-6. Statements 2 (decline) and
  # 5 (little to look forward to) are negatively worded, so they are reversed (7 minus the answer).
  # The score is the mean of the six items: 1 to 6, higher = more positive view of menopause.
  if (all(mindset_items %in% names(dat))) {
    dat <- dat |>
      mutate(mindset_score = (mindset_opportunity + (7 - mindset_decline) + mindset_important +
                              mindset_enjoyable + (7 - mindset_nothing_to_look_forward) +
                              mindset_manageable) / 6)
  }

  # Exclusion rule (the same one written in the Analysis plan). We KEEP a person only if:
  #  - they were assigned to normal or distress (the pilot also had a third group, which is
  #    now NA and is dropped),
  #  - they are 40 or older,
  #  - they said they are in perimenopause or postmenopause,
  #  - they took at least 2.5 minutes (the original study's rule),
  #  - they report 20 or fewer years of education after age 16.
  # (People who did not complete the study were already removed above.)
  # In pilot mode (see the pilot switch at the top) the age, menopause, time and education
  # rules are skipped, because Pilot A testers did not have to be eligible women.
  # (A completed session with no worry rating, for example an old test session, cannot be
  # analysed, so it is also dropped.)
  keep <- dat |> filter(!is.na(condition), !is.na(worried))
  if (!pilot_mode) {
    keep <- keep |>
      filter(age >= 40,
             menopause_stage %in% c("peri", "post"),
             minutes >= 2.5,
             education_years <= 20)
  }

  # Stopping rule: keep only the first max_n people who passed, in the order they started.
  # slice_head() takes the first rows, so the people are sorted by start time first.
  # n_passed remembers how many passed in total, before the cut, so the Methods can report it.
  n_passed <- nrow(keep)
  passed <- keep    # everyone who passed the exclusion rule, before the first-max_n cut
  keep <- keep |> arrange(lubridate::ymd_hms(started_at))
  if (is.finite(max_n)) keep <- keep |> slice_head(n = max_n)

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors,
       complete = complete, dat = dat, keep = keep, n_passed = n_passed, passed = passed,
       n_refused = sum(participants$participant_id %in% refused),
       n_not_menopausal = sum(dat$menopause_stage %in% "not"))
}

# Fit the ordinal logistic regression for ONE outcome (for example "worried"): the rating
# predicted by condition (normal is the comparison group) plus the three control variables (age, education, social media use).
# Returns one row per non-normal condition, or NULL if the model cannot be fitted yet
# (for example while there are only a few pilot participants).
fit_outcome <- function(dat, outcome) {
  d <- dat |>
    select(all_of(outcome), condition, age, education_years, social_media_use, menopause_stage) |>
    rename(y = all_of(outcome)) |>
    drop_na() |>
    mutate(y = factor(y, ordered = TRUE), condition = droplevels(condition))
  # The model: condition plus three control variables (age, education, social media use), the
  # same model as the original authors' script (their code scales each control with scale()).
  # Menopause stage is not a control: it was a screening criterion in the original. In pilot mode there are too few
  # people for four extra variables (the model cannot find a solution with about 10 rows),
  # so the pilot model uses condition only. The real study uses the full model.
  model_formula <- if (pilot_mode) y ~ condition else
    y ~ condition + scale(age) + scale(education_years) + scale(social_media_use)
  if (nrow(d) < min_n || nlevels(d$condition) < 2 || nlevels(d$y) < 2) return(NULL)
  m <- tryCatch(
    MASS::polr(model_formula, data = d, Hess = TRUE),
    error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(m)) return(NULL)
  broom::tidy(m) |>
    filter(coef.type == "coefficient", startsWith(term, "condition")) |>
    transmute(outcome = outcome,
              contrast = sub("^condition", "", term),
              N = nrow(d),
              beta = estimate, se = std.error, z = statistic,
              p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(statistic)),
              ci_low = beta - 1.96 * se, ci_high = beta + 1.96 * se)
}

# The key statistic: worried, distress vs normal. NULL until the model can be fitted.
key_result <- function(d) {
  r <- fit_outcome(d$keep, "worried")
  if (is.null(r)) return(NULL)
  r |> filter(contrast == "distress")
}

# All the secondary outcomes with the same model, distress vs normal.
outcomes <- c("worried", "reassured", "confused", "optimistic", "anxious",
              "empowered", "knowledgeable", "liked")
all_results <- function(d) {
  res <- map_dfr(outcomes, function(o) {
    r <- fit_outcome(d$keep, o)
    if (is.null(r)) tibble() else r
  })
  if (nrow(res) == 0) return(NULL)
  res |> filter(contrast == "distress")
}

# Side-by-side figure: the effect (beta, distress vs normal) with its 95% interval for each
# outcome, original and replication on the same axes. Positive = distress group rated higher.
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(ci_low = beta - 1.96 * se, ci_high = beta + 1.96 * se,
           Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
           outcome = factor(outcome, levels = rev(outcomes)))
  fills <- setNames(c("grey55", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  ggplot(df, aes(x = outcome, y = beta, colour = Study)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = fills) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Effect of distress vs normal (ordinal logistic β, 95% CI)", colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id, analysis_n)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2, analysis_n2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
# TRUE only when Phase 2 has at least min_n analysed participants (the models need enough data).
have_phase2_ok <- have_phase2 && nrow(phase2$keep) >= min_n
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_row <- function(study, r) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `β` = "not yet collected", SE = "",
                  `95% CI` = "", z = "", p = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `β` = sprintf("%.3f", r$beta), SE = sprintf("%.3f", r$se),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
         z = sprintf("%.2f", r$z),
         p = format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001))
}
original_row <- original_key |>
  transmute(N = sum(orig_n), beta, se, z, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(z)),
            ci_low = beta - 1.96 * se, ci_high = beta + 1.96 * se)
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original", original_row),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) key_result(phase1)),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) key_result(phase2))
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrrr",
               caption = paste0("Key comparison: effect of distress vs normal posts on worry (ordinal logistic regression, ", model_note, ")."))
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

The original study found that showing social media posts to peri- and
postmenopausal women framing the menopause transition as either normal,
distressful, or transformative had immediate effects on affective
responses (Osborne et al., 2026). Participants who viewed
distress-framed posts reported greater levels of worry and confusion,
and lower levels of reassurance, optimism, and empowerment.
Interestingly, the distress-framed posts increased perceived knowledge
of menopause, despite participants feeling more negatively toward them.
I replicated the study with only two conditions (normal vs. distress) to
examine the main finding of the original study. I used the same scales
to measure affective reactions, expected behavioral responses, and
perceptions. This study was important for me because it demonstrates how
narrative framing shapes affective responses and the importance of
choosing the right words to share medical information, especially for a
stage of life that half of the population will live through for almost
40% of their lives. Negative framing could also affect how women
experience their symptoms physically. I would like to further
investigate the mind-body effects of menopausal mindsets in the future.

One challenge that I anticipated was getting the original materials from
the authors, but they shared their original posts with me. They also
shared their data and analysis code on OSF. This helped me understand
their analysis and prepare my replication. For the statistical analysis,
I used ordinal logistic regression.

In Phase 2, I will compare how anxious participants feel right after
reading posts that describe menopause as a normal transition or as a
distressing experience.

## Methods

### Power analysis

```{r}
#| label: power
# Cohen's d for worry (distress vs normal) from the original data: the difference in means
# divided by the pooled standard deviation. The course template instead converts the
# log-odds beta with beta / (pi / sqrt(3)), which gives about 0.50 (an approximation that
# ignores the control variables). The direct calculation from the means is used here.
pooled_sd <- with(orig_worry, sqrt(sum((n - 1) * sd^2) / (sum(n) - 2)))
d_orig <- diff(orig_worry$mean) / pooled_sd

# The original study used p < .01, so power is calculated for alpha = .01.
power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n <- power.t.test(delta = d_orig, sd = 1, sig.level = 0.01, power = pw)$n
  tibble(power = scales::percent(pw), n_per_group = ceiling(n), n_total = 2 * ceiling(n))
})

# 2.5 times the original sample in the two groups of the key test (normal and distress).
two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * orig_n[c("normal", "distress")])

knitr::kable(power_rows, col.names = c("Power", "N per condition", "N total"),
             caption = sprintf(
               "Sample needed to detect the original effect on worry (beta = %.3f, about d = %.2f), two-sided alpha = .01, two conditions (normal vs distress).",
               original_key$beta, d_orig))
```

```{r}
#| label: power-proposed
# How much power does the sample I plan to collect have? The first row uses the original
# effect. The other rows ask "what if the true effect is smaller than the original?",
# because original effects are often overestimates.
proposed_per_group <- 130   # my planned N per condition (change this if the plan changes)

power_check <- tibble(
  effect = c("Original effect", "75% of the original", "Half of the original"),
  d      = d_orig * c(1, 0.75, 0.5)
) |>
  mutate(
    # power.t.test() with n filled in (and power left out) returns the power
    power = map_dbl(d, ~ power.t.test(n = proposed_per_group, delta = .x,
                                      sd = 1, sig.level = 0.01)$power),
    d     = round(d, 2),
    power = scales::percent(power, accuracy = 1)
  )

knitr::kable(power_check,
             col.names = c("True effect", "Cohen's d", "Power"),
             caption = sprintf("Power of %d participants per condition (alpha = .01) if the true effect was as large as, or smaller than, the original.",
                               proposed_per_group))
```

The original effect for the worry question comparing the distress and
normal conditions was β = .910. Cohen’s d was calculated using the means
and standard deviations of the two groups in the original data. This
gave a d of about 0.44.

With an alpha of .01, about 157 participants per group would be needed
to have 90% power to detect this effect. I chose 130 participants per
group because of resource constraints. With this sample, the power was
about 82% to detect an effect of d = 0.44. However, the true effect
could have been smaller than the one found in the original study.

### Planned sample

I planned to recruit women aged 40 or older from the UK through Prolific
who were perimenopausal or postmenopausal. The planned sample was 260
participants, with 130 in each condition. Participants who did not pass
the eligibility check did not count toward the 260.

Recruitment stopped when data from 260 people who passed the
inclusion/exclusion criteria had been collected.

### Materials

The original study used 12 social media posts, with four posts for each
narrative: normal, distress, and transformative. This replication study
used only the original posts from the normal and distress conditions.
Each participant saw four posts from their assigned condition. The study
included basic sociodemographic questions and questions about menopause
stage, HRT experience, perceived menopause knowledge, and social media
use. After viewing the posts, participants answered the original
questions about their affective responses, expected behavioral
responses, and perceptions of the posts.

Materials available at the following link:
https://psych251.github.io/osborne2026/

### Procedure

Participants recruited through Prolific first saw a consent page and
then answered basic sociodemographic and clinical questions about their
menopause. After the demographics page, their age and answer to the
original menopause question were used to check if they could
participate. Participants under 40 or who were not perimenopausal or
postmenopausal could not continue and were sent back to Prolific. The
condition was randomly assigned when they started the study, before the
demographic questions. Eligible participants then saw four posts
presenting menopause as either a distressing or a “normal” experience,
depending on their condition. The authors shared their original posts to
use in this replication. The posts were anonymized, standardized, and
copied from public X, Instagram, and Facebook posts. Participants
answered questions about the message of the posts, how the posts made
them feel (worried, reassured, confused, optimistic), their behavioral
intentions (like, share, save, comment, search, discuss), and their
perceptions of the posts (likability, credibility, trustworthiness,
representativeness). As far as I could tell from the original data, the
questions followed the same order. I included only two groups, normal
and distress, instead of three because of resource constraints. The
transformative posts were not included. I used a jsPsych website instead
of Qualtrics to run the experiment.

### Analysis plan

As in the original study, statistical analyses were done using R. The
packages apaTables, ggplot2, psych, and tidyverse were used for data
processing, analysis, and visualization.

Participant characteristics, HRT experience, perceived menopause
knowledge, and social media engagement were described using descriptive
statistics. Categorical variables were presented as counts and
percentages. Continuous variables were presented as means, SDs, and
ranges. Ordinal logistic regression was used because the outcomes were
measured on ordered 5-point Likert-type scales. The models examined the
impact of experimental condition on affective, behavioral, and
perceptual responses to the posts, using the normal narrative condition
as the reference category. Models controlled for age, years of education
after age 16, and frequency of social media use. Following the original
authors, I used P \< .01 as the significance threshold.

**Key analysis of interest.** My key analysis of interest was to compare
worry ratings between the distress and normal conditions using ordinal
logistic regression. In the original study, compared to participants who
viewed posts portraying menopause as normal, those who viewed distress
posts reported to be more worried about menopause (β = .910; SE = .170;
Wald z = 5.350; P \< .001; Osborne et al., 2026).

The key test was an ordinal logistic regression of the worry question on
condition, with the same three controls. The normal condition was the
reference group. The effect size was β (log-odds) for distress vs
normal, with a 95% confidence interval.

**Secondary outcomes.** Feeling reassured, confused, optimistic,
anxious, empowered, and knowledgeable, and how much participants liked
the posts, were also examined using the same ordinal logistic regression
model and covariates.

**Exclusions.** Participants were excluded if they did not complete the
study, completed the survey in less than 2.5 minutes, or reported more
than 20 years of education after age 16. The original research team
considered less than 2.5 minutes insufficient time to read and process
the survey content.

Participants were also excluded if they were not perimenopausal or
postmenopausal women. Participants younger than 40 years old were also
excluded.

### Differences from the original study

| Feature | Original study | Replication study | Could this influence the results? |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Number of groups | 3 (normal, distress, transformative) | 2 (normal, distress) | I did not expect this to affect the main comparison because my study focused on distress versus normal posts. |
| Platform | Qualtrics | jsPsych website | Probably not. The questions and posts were the same. As far as I could tell from the available materials, their order was also the same. |
| Sample size | 737 participants were analyzed, about 245 per group. | 260 participants, 130 per group. | The smaller sample gave less precise estimates. My sample had about 82% power to detect an effect of d = 0.44 with an alpha of .01. |
| Sample and pay | Prolific, UK women 40+, perimenopausal or postmenopausal, paid £1.50. | Prolific, UK women meeting the same age and menopause criteria. Paid about \$8 per hour. | Possibly. Payment differences could affect who participates. |
| 60-second wait | The data showed that participants in the normal and transformative groups stayed on the posts page for at least 60 seconds. However, about half of the distress group spent less than 60 seconds. I did not know why. | The Continue button was locked for 60 seconds. I added a bold instruction because some pilot participants missed it and thought the website was not working. | Possibly. Participants in my distress condition may have spent more time looking at the posts than participants in the original study. |

```{r}
#| label: pilot-checks
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Pilot checks: how many people dropped out, were screened out, and how long the study took.
# Each number is computed from the exported participants table (one row per person who
# opened the study). "completed" is TRUE only for people who reached the end.
n_started <- nrow(participants)
n_done    <- nrow(complete)
n_refused <- phase1$n_refused   # declined the consent form (not counted as completers)
# The "screened_out" column is saved for people the in-study screening sent away. If the
# export has no such column, we count them as 0 and say so in the table note.
n_screened <- if ("screened_out" %in% names(participants)) sum(participants$screened_out %in% TRUE) else 0
# Dropouts = started, but neither finished nor screened out.
n_dropped <- n_started - n_done - n_screened - n_refused

# Instruction clarity (1-5), answered by people who finished. jsPsych saves 0-4, so add 1.
clarity <- parse_task(trials |> filter(participant_id %in% complete$participant_id),
                      "feedback_likert")
clarity_mean <- if ("instructions_clear" %in% names(clarity))
  mean(as.numeric(clarity$instructions_clear) + 1, na.rm = TRUE) else NA

tibble(
  Measure = c("Started", "Screened out (not eligible)", "Declined consent", "Dropped out", "Completed",
              "Dropout among eligible starters (%)",
              "Median minutes (completers)", "Fastest / slowest (minutes)",
              "Mean instruction clarity (1-5)", "Browser error reports"),
  Value = c(n_started, n_screened, n_refused, n_dropped, n_done,
            round(100 * n_dropped / max(n_started - n_screened, 1), 1),
            round(median(complete$minutes), 1),
            paste(round(min(complete$minutes), 1), "/", round(max(complete$minutes), 1)),
            round(clarity_mean, 2), nrow(errors))
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Pilot checks.")
```

#### Deviations from the preregistered plan

In Phase 1, I used jsPsych instead of Qualtrics to run the experiment.
The data export initially marked five people who declined consent as
having completed the study. I removed them from the completion count.
After applying my analysis criteria, I had 265 eligible people that
completed the study and the first 260 (130 per group) were analyzed, as
I preregistered it.

## Results

### Data preparation

A total of 266 participants completed the experiment, and 265 met the
criteria for analysis. I analyzed the first 260 eligible completers (130
per group), following my preregistered stopping rule.

### Confirmatory analysis

For my main analysis, I used ordinal logistic regression to examine
whether distressing menopause posts increased worry compared to normal
posts. I controlled for age, education, and social media use, as the
authors of the original study did.

The effect of distressing posts on worry was β = 0.97 (SE = 0.23), with
Cohen’s d = 0.54 without controlling for other variables. After
controlling for age, education, and social media use, the effect was
larger, β = 1.245 (SE = 0.243, p \< .001), with a d of 0.63. Most of the
change came from the covariate age because participants in the distress
condition were slightly older.

Cohen’s d was calculated by dividing the difference between the two
group means by the pooled standard deviation.

```{r}
#| label: cohens-d
#| eval: !expr have_data
g <- keep |>                         # keep = the 260 analysed participants
  group_by(condition) |>             # split into normal and distress
  summarise(m = mean(worried),       # average worry in each group
            s = sd(worried),         # spread (SD) in each group
            n = n())                 # people in each group
sp <- sqrt(((g$n[1] - 1) * g$s[1]^2 + (g$n[2] - 1) * g$s[2]^2) /
           (g$n[1] + g$n[2] - 2))    # pooled SD: the groups' SDs combined, weighted by size
d <- (g$m[g$condition == "distress"] - g$m[g$condition == "normal"]) / sp
round(d, 2)                          # difference in means divided by pooled SD
```

```{r}
#| label: effect-without-and-with-controls
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Beta WITHOUT controls: same ordinal model, but condition is the only predictor.
m0 <- MASS::polr(factor(worried, ordered = TRUE) ~ condition, data = keep, Hess = TRUE)
round(coef(summary(m0))["conditiondistress", c("Value", "Std. Error")], 2)   # beta and its SE

# Cohen's d WITH controls: a linear model with condition + the three controls.
# The condition coefficient is the adjusted difference between groups (in rating points);
# sigma() is the spread left after the controls, so dividing gives d in standard-deviation units.
ols <- lm(worried ~ condition + scale(age) + scale(education_years) + scale(social_media_use),
          data = keep)
round(coef(ols)["conditiondistress"] / sigma(ols), 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
# The confirmatory test: worried, distress vs normal.
res_key <- key_result(phase1)
if (!is.null(res_key)) {
  res_key |>
    transmute(N, Beta = round(beta, 3), SE = round(se, 3), z = round(z, 2),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Ordinal logistic regression: effect of distress vs normal posts on worry.")
} else {
  message("The model was not fitted: it needs at least 20 analysed participants, in at least two conditions.")
}

# The other outcomes, with the same model (secondary analyses), next to the original.
res_all <- all_results(phase1)
if (!is.null(res_all)) {
  res_all |>
    left_join(original |> select(outcome, orig_beta = beta, orig_se = se), by = "outcome") |>
    transmute(Outcome = outcome,
              `Original beta (SE)` = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", orig_beta, orig_se),
              `Replication beta (SE)` = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", beta, se),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Secondary outcomes: distress vs normal, same model as the key test.")
}
```

### Replication assessment

The authors of the original study reported β = 0.910, SE = 0.170, and d
≈ 0.44, while my effect was slightly larger, β = 1.245 and d ≈ 0.54.

My 95% confidence interval was \[0.77, 1.72\], and it included the
original estimate of 0.910. My results are consistent with the original
findings.

At the .01 threshold that the authors used, I replicated the effects on
feeling confused, optimistic, anxious, and knowledgeable. The effects on
feeling reassured (p = .029), liking the posts (p = .084), and feeling
empowered (p = .58) were in the same direction as in the original study,
but they were smaller and did not meet the threshold.

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- original_row
rep  <- key_result(phase1)

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Effect (beta)` = sprintf("%.3f", beta),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: effect of distress vs normal posts on worry (ordinal logistic beta).")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: the model needs at least 20 analysed participants in at least two conditions.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$ci_low > 0 | rep$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$beta >= rep$ci_low & orig$beta <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.3f. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    orig$beta))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

```{r}
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Effect of distress vs normal posts on each outcome, original study and Phase 1 replication (ordinal logistic beta). Bars are 95% confidence intervals. Positive means the distress group rated higher."
#| fig-width: 7
```


## Discussion

### Summary of replication attempt

I consider this a successful replication. I found a significant effect
in the same direction as the original study, with a slightly larger
effect size (d = 0.54 vs. d = 0.44), even though my sample was about
half the size of the two compared groups in the original study. My
confidence interval also included the original effect estimate.

### Commentary

Two differences may help explain why the worry effect was larger in my
study. In the original study, 55.8% of participants in the distress
condition left the page with the posts before 60 seconds, compared with
0% in my study. Also, 43% of participants in my normal condition
selected the lowest worry rating (1), compared with 14.5% in the
original study.

# Phase 2: Extension

**Track:** Best-practices upgrade (metascience)

## Rationale

Although my replication was successful, I think I can improve the
precision of my results. In Phase 1, the worry variable was assessed by
asking one Likert-style question.

For Phase 2, I want to increase the sample and add some measures to make
the worry measurement more robust.

## Changes from Phase 1

I want to add the STAI-6, expected symptom severity (“How severe do you
expect your menopause symptoms to be over the next four weeks?”), a
menopause word association task (the first 3 words that come to mind), and a six-item measure of menopause mindsets.

I will keep the original procedure from phase 1 the same. The new measures will be added at the end of the survey.

| Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Sample | 260 participants (130 per group) | About 386 participants (193 per group) | I want a larger sample to get a more precise estimate and reduce my standard error. |
| Instructions | The survey takes about 6 minutes. | The survey takes about 10 minutes. | The new questions and the word association task add time to the survey. |
| Measurement | None | STAI-6, as a primary measure along with worry | There is no well-validated scale for menopause-related worry, so I'll use the STAI-6 to make the measurement more robust. |
| Exploratory measure | None | Expected symptom severity | I want to see if the posts change how severe women expect their menopause symptoms to be. |
| Exploratory measure | None | Word associations (first three words about menopause) | I want to see if the words that come to women's minds differ between conditions. |
| Exploratory measure | None | Menopause mindsets (6 items rated from 1 = strongly disagree to 6 = strongly agree) | I want to see if women’s beliefs about menopause differ between the two groups after reading the posts. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

For Phase 2, I plan to recruit around 193 participants per group, for a
total of approximately 386 participants.

With this sample, I expect a standard error of around 0.20, compared to
0.243 in Phase 1. This should give me a narrower confidence interval and
a more precise estimate.

My estimated budget is around \$910.

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
#| eval: false
phase2_n_per_group <- 193   # planned analysed participants per condition in Phase 2

p1_counts <- if (have_data) risky_counts(phase1)
p1_stats  <- if (have_data) diff_ci(p1_counts)
basis <- if (!is.null(p1_stats)) {
  list(gain = p1_counts$risky[p1_counts$condition == "gain"] / p1_counts$n[p1_counts$condition == "gain"],
       loss = p1_counts$risky[p1_counts$condition == "loss"] / p1_counts$n[p1_counts$condition == "loss"],
       source = "Phase 1")
} else {
  list(gain = original_p_gain, loss = original_p_loss, source = "the original study")
}

# Expected 95% CI half-width on the difference at n per condition.
half_width <- function(n) 1.96 * sqrt(basis$gain * (1 - basis$gain) / n + basis$loss * (1 - basis$loss) / n)
power_at <- function(n, p1, p2) {
  tryCatch(power.prop.test(n = n, p1 = p1, p2 = p2, sig.level = 0.05)$power, error = function(e) NA)
}

rows <- tibble(
  Study = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) "Phase 1 (actual)", "Phase 2 (planned)"),
  `N analysed` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) p1_stats$N, 2 * phase2_n_per_group),
  `95% CI half-width` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("±%.0f points", 100 * (p1_stats$ci_high - p1_stats$ci_low) / 2),
                          sprintf("±%.0f points (expected)", 100 * half_width(phase2_n_per_group)))
)
knitr::kable(rows, caption = sprintf("Precision of the key estimate, Phase 2 expected values based on %s.", basis$source))

tibble(
  `Effect to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: %.0f points", 100 * (original_p_loss - original_p_gain)),
                         if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("Phase 1: %.0f points", 100 * p1_stats$estimate),
                         sprintf("Half the original: %.0f points", 50 * (original_p_loss - original_p_gain))),
  `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(c(
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, original_p_gain, original_p_loss),
    if (!is.null(p1_stats)) power_at(phase2_n_per_group, basis$gain, basis$loss),
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, original_p_gain, original_p_gain + (original_p_loss - original_p_gain) / 2)
  ), accuracy = 1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Power of the Phase 2 key test at %d per condition, two-sided alpha = .05.", phase2_n_per_group))
```

## Analysis plan

I will use the same main analysis as in Phase 1: ordinal logistic
regression predicting worry from the experimental condition, controlling
for age, education, and social media use.

I will use the same exclusion criteria as in Phase 1.

Participants will be included if they finish the study and pass the same criteria as in Phase 1. Recruitment will stop at 386 participants who meet these criteria. About 193 are expected in each group. If more than 386 qualify, the first 386 by start time will be analyzed.

Participants are assigned to a group before they answer the eligibility questions. For each group, a table will show how many were assigned, were not eligible, did not finish after passing the eligibility questions, finished, and were included in the analysis.

I will also analyze STAI-6 as an additional primary measure.  An expected symptom severity question, a menopause mindset scale and word associations will be included as exploratory measures.

The STAI-6 consists of six items rated from 1 to 4. The items “calm,”
“relaxed,” and “content” will be reverse-scored. The six item scores
will then be summed, multiplied by 20, and then divided by 6 to obtain a
score range from 20 to 80 as the complete STAI scale. Higher scores
indicate higher state anxiety.

The STAI-6 comes after all of the study’s original questions. Because it comes later, the effect may be smaller than d = 0.35. With 193 participants per group, the study has about 80% power to detect an effect of d = 0.35 with a two-sided test at α = .01. If the result is not significant, a smaller effect is still possible.

The Menopause Mindset Scale is a six item scale (agree/disagree) I have
created from my clinical experience. The items 2 and 5 are reversed. The score of the scale would be obtained from the average. The alpha would be evaluated.

The instruction in the survey is “Please indicate how much you agree or disagree with each statement about menopause.”

1. Menopause is an opportunity to grow and to continue building my life.
2. Menopause marks an overall decline in the life of a woman.
3. Achieving menopause is a peak experience in a woman’s life.
4. Even though there are obstacles, menopause is an enjoyable stage of life.
5. When a woman reaches menopause, she has little left to look forward to in life.
6. Menopause symptoms are manageable, and I can treat them to live well.

The same answers are used for all six items. Strongly disagree (1), Disagree (2), Somewhat disagree (3), Somewhat agree (4), Agree (5), and Strongly agree (6).

The survey saves the answers as numbers from 0 to 5. One point will be added to each number. Then items 2 and 5 will be scored as 7 minus the new number. The final score will be the average of the six items. It goes from 1 to 6. A higher score means a more positive view of menopause.

Cronbach’s alpha will be reported for the six items. The results for each item will also be shown separately. This will help show how participants answered each item if alpha is low.

After the original measures, participants will complete the new measures in this order: STAI-6, word associations, the expected symptom severity item, and menopause mindsets. The most common words will be reported for each condition, along with the percentage of participants who mentioned each word. The comparison will be exploratory.

**Word association task**

Responses will be changed to lowercase automatically. Claude Sonnet 5.5 will be used once to suggest spelling corrections, before the two groups are compared. The model will get a list of all the word association responses in alphabetical order. Each response will appear only once. The model will only return responses that seem to have spelling mistakes, with a suggested correction for each one. The list will have no participant IDs or group labels.

I will check the suggested changes without seeing the group labels. Only clear spelling corrections will be changed. The same correction will be used every time the same response appears. The exact prompt, model name, date of the run, and final table of original and corrected responses will be saved in the repository and on OSF.

After the spelling check, each response will be searched in AFINN. If a single word is not found, its base form will be searched. For example, if “flashes” is not found, “flash” will be searched. A response like “hot flashes” will be searched as one phrase. If the phrase is not found, it will get no score. The versions of AFINN, R, and the R packages used for scoring will be recorded. The number of participants with a score will be reported for each group.

Exact prompt:

> Check these responses for clear spelling mistakes in English. Each line is one response. If there is a clear spelling mistake, fix only the spelling. If the intended word is unclear, keep the response as it is. Keep phrases together. Do not add or remove words, replace a word with a synonym, or change a word to its base form. Both British and American spellings are accepted. Do not change a correct British spelling to American spelling, or the other way around. Return a table with two columns, `original_response` and `corrected_response`. Include only the responses that were changed. Copy the original response exactly in the first column.

**Exploratory outcomes**

* Expected symptom severity. I expect participants who see the distress-focused posts to expect more severe menopause symptoms over the next four weeks. I will use ordinal logistic regression for this item, with group as the predictor.
* Menopause mindsets. I expect participants who see the distress-focused posts to have less positive mindsets about menopause. I will reverse-score items 2 and 5 and average all six items for each participant. Higher scores mean a more positive mindset. I will compare the group means with a Welch t-test.
* Word associations. I expect participants who see the distress-focused posts to use more negative words to describe menopause. I will put the words in lowercase and remove extra spaces. I will look up each of the three words in AFINN (via the tidytext package in R) as the participant wrote it after the spelling check. If a word is not in AFINN, I will look up its base form instead (for example, "flash" for "flashes"). I will average the scores of the words that match. If none match, the participant's score will be missing for this analysis. I will report how many words matched in each group and compare the group means with a Welch t-test.

All three analyses are exploratory. I will report the odds ratio for expected symptom severity and the mean differences for mindsets and word valence, all with 95% confidence intervals. I will report unadjusted p-values and interpret the results as exploratory. If I also test individual words, I will use the Holm correction across those tests, among words given by at least 5% of participants.

Linear regression will be used to test whether STAI-6 scores differ by
condition, controlling for age, education, and social media use.

The expected effect size is about d = 0.35, based on the effect observed
for the “anxious” item in Phase 1. With 193 participants per group, the estimated power to detect this effect is about 80% considering α = .01.

The effect on worry is expected to go in the same direction and be about the same size as in Phase 1. The standard error is expected to be smaller, about 0.20, because Phase 2 has more participants.

Fixed-sequence testing will be used. The effect of condition on worry
will be tested first at α = .01. The effect on STAI-6 scores will be
tested at α = .01 only if the worry test is significant. If not, the
STAI-6 analysis will be reported as exploratory.

If I combine the results from Phase 1 and Phase 2, I will report this as
an exploratory analysis.

My new experiment ID will be `osborne2026-extension`.

```{r}
#| label: phase2-counts
#| eval: !expr have_phase2
# How many people started, completed and were analysed in Phase 2.
cat(sprintf("Phase 2: %d started, %d completed, %d analysed.\n",
            nrow(phase2$participants), nrow(phase2$complete), nrow(phase2$keep)))
```

```{r}
#| label: phase2-worry
#| eval: !expr have_phase2
# TEST 1 of the fixed sequence: worry, distress vs normal, alpha = .01 (same model as Phase 1).
res_worry2 <- key_result(phase2)
if (!is.null(res_worry2)) {
  res_worry2 |>
    transmute(N, Beta = round(beta, 3), SE = round(se, 3), z = round(z, 2),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Phase 2, test 1: effect of distress vs normal posts on worry (ordinal logistic regression).")
}
# Is test 1 significant at alpha = .01? This decides whether test 2 (STAI-6) is confirmatory.
# The gate needs both: p < .01 AND the effect in the expected direction (beta > 0 = distress worried more).
worry_significant <- !is.null(res_worry2) && res_worry2$p < 0.01 && res_worry2$beta > 0
```

```{r}
#| label: phase2-stai
#| eval: !expr have_phase2_ok
# TEST 2 of the fixed sequence: STAI-6 score (20 to 80), distress vs normal, alpha = .01.
# Linear regression: the score predicted by condition plus the same three controls.
k2 <- phase2$keep
ols_stai <- lm(stai_score ~ condition + scale(age) + scale(education_years) + scale(social_media_use),
               data = k2)
b    <- coef(summary(ols_stai))["conditiondistress", ]      # estimate, SE, t, p
ci   <- confint(ols_stai, "conditiondistress", level = 0.99)  # 99% CI to match alpha = .01
d_st <- b["Estimate"] / sigma(ols_stai)                      # adjusted Cohen's d (same idea as Phase 1)
tibble(N = nrow(k2),
       `Difference (points)` = round(unname(b["Estimate"]), 2),
       SE = round(unname(b["Std. Error"]), 2),
       `99% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci[1], ci[2]),
       p = format.pval(unname(b["Pr(>|t|)"]), digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
       `Cohen's d` = round(unname(d_st), 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Phase 2, test 2: effect of distress vs normal posts on the STAI-6 score.")
# The fixed-sequence rule: test 2 counts as confirmatory only if test 1 was significant.
if (worry_significant) {
  cat("Worry was significant at alpha = .01, so the STAI-6 test is confirmatory (alpha = .01).\n")
} else {
  cat("Worry was not significant at alpha = .01, so the STAI-6 analysis is exploratory.\n")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: phase2-exploratory
#| eval: !expr have_phase2_ok
# EXPLORATORY measures (descriptive only): symptom severity (0-4) and the six mindset items (1-6),
# mean and SD in each condition.
k2 |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  summarise(n = n(), across(any_of(c("symptom_severity", mindset_items)),
                            list(m = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), s = ~ sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(condition, n), names_to = c("measure", ".value"), names_pattern = "(.*)_(m|s)$") |>
  mutate(across(c(m, s), ~ round(.x, 2))) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Condition", "N", "Measure", "Mean", "SD"),
               caption = "Phase 2, exploratory: symptom severity and menopause mindsets by condition (descriptive).")

# Mindset score (mean of the six items after reversing statements 2 and 5, 1 to 6): mean and SD by condition.
k2 |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  summarise(N = n(), Mean = round(mean(mindset_score, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
            SD = round(sd(mindset_score, na.rm = TRUE), 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Phase 2, exploratory: menopause mindset score (1 to 6, higher = more positive) by condition.")

# Reliability of the new scale: Cronbach's alpha (do the six items move together?).
mindset_items_scored <- k2 |>
  transmute(opportunity = mindset_opportunity, decline = 7 - mindset_decline,
            important = mindset_important, enjoyable = mindset_enjoyable,
            no_future = 7 - mindset_nothing_to_look_forward, manageable = mindset_manageable)
cat(sprintf("Cronbach's alpha of the mindset score: %.2f\n",
            psych::alpha(mindset_items_scored, check.keys = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha))

# ---- Exploratory test 1: expected symptom severity (ordinal logistic regression, group only) ----
# polr() fits the proportional-odds model; exp(beta) is the odds ratio for distress vs normal.
sev <- k2 |> select(symptom_severity, condition) |> drop_na() |>
  mutate(symptom_severity = factor(symptom_severity, ordered = TRUE), condition = droplevels(condition))
if (nrow(sev) >= 2 && nlevels(sev$condition) == 2 && nlevels(sev$symptom_severity) >= 2) {
  m_sev <- MASS::polr(symptom_severity ~ condition, data = sev, Hess = TRUE)
  b_sev <- coef(summary(m_sev))["conditiondistress", ]
  tibble(N = nrow(sev),
         `Odds ratio` = round(exp(b_sev["Value"]), 2),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", exp(b_sev["Value"] - 1.96 * b_sev["Std. Error"]),
                                             exp(b_sev["Value"] + 1.96 * b_sev["Std. Error"])),
         p = format.pval(2 * pnorm(-abs(b_sev["t value"])), digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Phase 2, exploratory: expected symptom severity, distress vs normal (ordinal logistic regression, unadjusted).")
}

# ---- Exploratory test 2: mindset score, Welch t-test ----
# t.test() uses the Welch version by default (var.equal = FALSE).
# The difference is computed as distress minus normal, with its 95% CI.
welch_row <- function(x_distress, x_normal, label) {
  tt <- t.test(x_distress, x_normal)                  # Welch: first group minus second group
  tibble(Outcome = label,
         `Mean distress` = round(mean(x_distress, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
         `Mean normal`   = round(mean(x_normal, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
         `N distress` = sum(!is.na(x_distress)), `N normal` = sum(!is.na(x_normal)),   # people with a score
         Difference = round(unname(tt$estimate[1] - tt$estimate[2]), 2),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", tt$conf.int[1], tt$conf.int[2]),
         p = format.pval(tt$p.value, digits = 2, eps = 0.001))
}
mind_tab <- welch_row(k2$mindset_score[k2$condition == "distress"],
                      k2$mindset_score[k2$condition == "normal"], "Mindset score (1 to 6)")

# ---- Word associations: clean the words, then top 10 per condition ----
# Cleaning: lowercase, trim spaces, base form (lemma). Obvious spelling errors must be fixed
# by hand before this step (for example with recode()).
words_clean <- parse_task(phase2$trials |> filter(participant_id %in% k2$participant_id),
                          "word_associations") |>
  left_join(k2 |> select(participant_id, condition), by = "participant_id") |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("word_"), values_to = "word") |>   # one row per word typed
  mutate(typed = str_to_lower(str_trim(word)),                # word as typed: lowercase, no extra spaces
         word  = textstem::lemmatize_words(typed)) |>         # base form: "flashes" becomes "flash"
  filter(!is.na(word), word != "") |>
  distinct(participant_id, condition, word, .keep_all = TRUE) # count each person once per word

words_by_cond <- words_clean |>
  count(condition, word, sort = TRUE, name = "n_people") |>   # how many people wrote each word
  left_join(k2 |> count(condition, name = "N"), by = "condition") |>  # people in each condition
  mutate(Percent = round(100 * n_people / N, 1)) |>           # percentage of participants
  group_by(condition) |> slice_head(n = 10) |>                # top 10 per condition
  select(condition, word, n_people, Percent)
knitr::kable(words_by_cond,
             caption = "Phase 2, exploratory: most common words by condition, and percentage of participants who mentioned each.")

# ---- Exploratory test 3: word valence with the AFINN dictionary (via tidytext) ----
# AFINN gives each English word a score from -5 (negative) to +5 (positive).
# The first time, R may ask to download it (package textdata): answer 1 / yes.
afinn <- tidytext::get_sentiments("afinn")
# Look up the word as typed first ("tired" is in AFINN, its base form "tire" is not);
# if that word is not in AFINN, look up its base form. coalesce() takes the first non-missing value.
word_scores <- words_clean |>
  left_join(afinn |> rename(value_typed = value), by = c("typed" = "word")) |>
  left_join(afinn |> rename(value_base  = value), by = "word") |>
  mutate(value = coalesce(value_typed, value_base))           # value = NA when neither is in AFINN
# Report how many words matched in each group.
word_scores |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  summarise(`Words` = n(), `Matched in AFINN` = sum(!is.na(value)),
            `% matched` = round(100 * mean(!is.na(value)), 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Phase 2, exploratory: words matched in AFINN, by condition.")
# One score per participant: the mean of the matched words (missing if none matched).
valence <- word_scores |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  group_by(participant_id, condition) |>
  summarise(valence = mean(value), .groups = "drop")
# How many people received a valence score (at least one matched word), per condition.
k2 |> count(condition, name = "People") |>
  left_join(valence |> count(condition, name = "Scored"), by = "condition") |>
  mutate(Scored = coalesce(Scored, 0L), `% scored` = round(100 * Scored / People, 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Phase 2, exploratory: participants who received a word-valence score, by condition.")
val_tab <- welch_row(valence$valence[valence$condition == "distress"],
                     valence$valence[valence$condition == "normal"], "Word valence (AFINN, -5 to +5)")

bind_rows(mind_tab, val_tab) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Phase 2, exploratory: group means, differences (distress minus normal), 95% CIs and unadjusted p-values (Welch t-tests).")

# ---- Optional: individual words said by at least 5% of participants, Holm-corrected ----
# Only run if you decide to test single words. Fisher's exact test per word, then Holm across them.
n_by_cond <- k2 |> count(condition, name = "N")
freq_words <- words_clean |> count(word) |> filter(n >= 0.05 * nrow(k2)) |> pull(word)
if (length(freq_words) > 0) {                 # only run if at least one word reaches 5% of participants
  word_tests <- map_dfr(freq_words, function(w) {
    said <- words_clean |> filter(word == w) |> count(condition, name = "yes")
    tab <- n_by_cond |> left_join(said, by = "condition") |> mutate(yes = coalesce(yes, 0L), no = N - yes)
    tibble(word = w, p = fisher.test(as.matrix(tab[, c("yes", "no")]))$p.value)
  }) |> mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p, method = "holm"))
  knitr::kable(word_tests |> mutate(across(c(p, p_holm), ~ format.pval(.x, digits = 2, eps = 0.001))),
               caption = "Phase 2, exploratory: individual words (at least 5% of participants), Fisher's exact test with Holm correction.")
} else {
  cat("No word was given by at least 5% of participants, so no single-word tests were run.\n")
}
```

## Discussion

# Data and code availability

The experiment code, the anonymized data, and the code that produces
every number in this report are available at
<https://github.com/psych251/osborne2026>. The experiment itself can be
taken at <https://psych251.github.io/osborne2026/>. The data contain no
names, email addresses, IP addresses, or Prolific IDs; the file linking
participants to their Prolific IDs is kept privately for payment and is
not shared.

Before uploading the Pilot B data, I removed two comments with personal
health information from trials.csv and export.json, following the course
guidelines. I put a short note instead "\[removed: personal details\]".
